results.title: OptimCLM: Optimizing clinical language models for predicting patient outcomes via knowledge distillation, pruning and quantization - ScienceDirect
results.content: # OptimCLM: Optimizing clinical language models for predicting patient outcomes via knowledge distillation, pruning and quantization. These challenges include: ***(i) Hardware limitations:*** Most healthcare facilities, especially smaller clinics and rural hospitals, lack access to high-end GPUs required for running large models, ***(ii) Latency constraints:*** Clinical decision-making often requires real-time predictions, but large models have significant inference delays, ***(iii) Resource management:*** Healthcare systems need to serve multiple departments simultaneously, making it impractical to deploy resource-intensive models across all units, and ***(iv) Edge deployment barriers:*** Many clinical settings require on-device inference due to privacy concerns or connectivity issues, but edge devices cannot handle large model footprints. This work demonstrates that carefully designed model compression techniques combining ensemble learning, knowledge distillation, pruning and quantization can make CLMs significantly more practical for real-world healthcare deployment while maintaining strong predictive performance. We fine-tune multiple pre-trained generalist and domain-adaptive LLMs on four clinical predictive tasks using the admission notes of the MIMIC-III clinical database, and select best two models by considering performance and domain-knowledge: DischargeBERT [74] and COReBERT [19].

# Model Compression, Quantization & Distillation. While large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized what’s possible with AI, their massive computational and memory demands pose serious challenges for deployment. This post explores three foundational techniques — **Model Compression**, **Quantization**, and **Knowledge Distillation** — that can significantly reduce model complexity without sacrificing core performance. ## I) Model Compression. Model compression refers to techniques that reduce a model’s memory footprint and computational requirements. This three-stage pipeline — **pruning**, **quantization**, and **Huffman encoding** — achieves up to a 49× reduction in model size without sacrificing accuracy. This illustration from the original MobileNet paper demonstrates how the model’s lightweight architecture — powered by depthwise separable convolutions — enables efficient deployment across mobile use cases such as object detection, face attribute recognition, fine-grained classification, and landmark recognition. * **Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)**: Models are trained with simulated quantization noise, leading to higher accuracy after deployment. >  Paper:* *Quantization and Training of Neural Networks*. results.title: Model Compression Techniques: Quantization, Pruning, Distillation, and Binarization
results.content: # Model Compression Techniques: Quantization, Pruning, Distillation, and Binarization. Model compression techniques aim to reduce the size and computational cost of large models while maintaining their predictive performance. Compression methods—by reducing model size and latency—facilitate broader adoption without sacrificing performance. Below is a detailed introduction on model compression techniques, focusing on four core methods: quantization, pruning, distillation, and binarization. Quantization reduces the precision of model weights and activations from high-precision floating-point numbers (e.g., 32-bit) to lower-precision representations (e.g., 8-bit), thereby decreasing memory footprint and speeding up computations. REFERENCE: Recent implementations have shown that 8-bit quantization can reduce model size by up to 75% while retaining most of the original accuracy (Jacob et al., 2018). Pruning involves eliminating weights or neurons that contribute little to model performance, creating sparse architectures that require fewer computations and less memory. REFERENCE: Empirical studies demonstrate that aggressive pruning (removing 90% or more of parameters) can still maintain near-original performance levels in many models (Han et al., 2015). Distillation transfers knowledge from a large “teacher” model to a smaller “student” model, enabling the student to approximate the teacher’s performance with far fewer parameters. (2015) demonstrated that a distilled student model could achieve performance close to its teacher while being significantly smaller and faster. While binarization offers the most extreme form of compression, it usually incurs a significant drop in model accuracy. (2016) showed that binarized neural networks can perform competitively on standard benchmarks, albeit with a trade-off between compression ratio and accuracy. Each model compression technique offers a unique balance between compression ratio and accuracy retention, and in practice, combinations of these methods are often employed to achieve optimal performance on resource-constrained devices. Quantization is effective for reducing precision while maintaining most performance, pruning removes redundancy, distillation transfers knowledge effectively, and binarization provides extreme compression at the cost of accuracy. REFERENCE: Comprehensive benchmarks in the literature show that combining these methods can lead to significant improvements in speed and memory usage without compromising accuracy substantially (Han et al., 2016; Hinton et al., 2015; Courbariaux et al., 2016). #AI #DataScience #data #generative ai #reinforcement learning optimization #model optimization techniques #fine tuning llms.

# Chapter 27: Model Compression Techniques. Successfully training a large language model often results in models with billions of parameters. While powerful, these models present significant challenges for practical deployment due to their large memory footprint (requiring substantial VRAMVRAMVRAM) and high computational cost during inference, which translates to latency and operational expense. This chapter addresses these challenges by introducing model compression techniques. These methods aim to reduce the size and computational demands of LLMs, making them more feasible to deploy, particularly in resource-constrained environments or applications requiring low latency. You will learn about several key strategies:. results.title: Quantization, Distillation and Pruning
results.content: This blog delves into cutting-edge model compression techniques such as quantization, pruning, and distillation, which aim to make NLP models more efficient without compromising their effectiveness. *   Post-training quantization can be problematic, as reducing precision can significantly impact the range of values that can be expressed, and simply rounding float values to binary (0 or 1) does not work for complex models. Distillation has emerged as a transformative technique in NLP, enabling the compression of large models into smaller, more efficient versions without significant performance loss. Unlike quantization and pruning, distillation fundamentally changes the architecture and parameters of a model. **Knowledge distillation** involves training a smaller model (student) to replicate the behavior of a larger one (teacher). The model distills itself multiple times, improving with each iteration i.e., Models generate and train on their own data, enabling tasks like instruction fine-tuning. *   **Self-Distillation with Synthetic Data**: Models generating and training on their own datasets promise further efficiency.
